result.summary: Pausanias describes Ionia: the founding of new Smyrna after Alexander's dream, and the temples of the region. He tells how the Erythraeans hauled Hercules' raft ashore with rope made of women's hair, then lists springs, rivers, baths and tombs.

scenes.title: Alexander founds new Smyrna
scenes.summary: Ionians take Smyrna from the Aeolians. Alexander, told in a dream by the Nemeses, founds the new city, and the Clarian oracle blesses the move.
scenes.stakes: The Smyrnaeans must decide whether to leave their old city; the oracle promises happiness if they move.

scenes.title: Temples of Ionia
scenes.summary: Pausanias praises the Ionian temples, including those burnt by the Persians, and the temples at Erythrae and Priene.

scenes.title: Raft of Hercules at Erythrae
scenes.summary: The raft of Hercules cannot be landed until the blind fisherman Phormio dreams of a rope of women's hair. Thracian women give theirs, the raft lands, and Phormio is healed.
scenes.stakes: The Erythraeans and Chians cannot land the sacred raft; Phormio is blind.

scenes.title: Statues, springs, baths and tombs
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the Erythraean statue of Athene, then the rivers, wells, baths, caves and tombs that make Ionia remarkable.

notable_quotes.reason: The Clarian oracle's blessing that persuaded the Smyrnaeans to move.

analysis.text: Pausanias links places to dreams, oracles and sacred objects, showing how divine signs shaped civic foundations and cult.
New Smyrna's refoundation, credited to Alexander, reflects Hellenistic city-building; Ionian temples show the region's wealth and Persian damage.

legacy.text: Smyrna, refounded on Mount Pagus, grew into a major Mediterranean port, today's Izmir.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says Thracian women alone may enter the Erythraean temple of Hercules, a ritual rule explained by the hair rope.

language_notes.text: The Pan-Ionic league was the federation of Ionian cities, which met at a shared festival; Smyrna's admission made it a member.
"In the present conjuncture" means in the current circumstances, that is, when facing the proposed move.
The Meles is a river near Smyrna. Claros was Apollo's oracle near Colophon, famous for verse responses.
"Opulence" means great richness; "Branchidæ" is the site of Apollo's temple near Miletus, "Milesia" being Miletus's territory.
The Persians burnt Ionian temples during their conquest and the Ionian revolt in the sixth and fifth centuries BC.
"Perfect Egyptian" means wholly Egyptian in style, unlike the Greek schools of Aegina and Attica.
The god is Hercules, who in this local tradition crossed from Tyre, where he was worshipped as the Phoenician Melqart, on a raft.
A distaff is a staff that holds wool or flax for spinning; it marks Athene as patron of women's work.
Endœus was an early Greek sculptor, said to have been a pupil of Daedalus; Pausanias attributes works to him on stylistic grounds.
The clause 'which is unmixed with any other water' is garbled; it seems to say the sea there is pure, unmixed with river water.
Biblis, in legend, fell in love with her brother Caunus and wept until she turned into a spring.
Pyrrhus is probably the son of Achilles; the local legend of him as a shepherd is not explained here.
Œnopion was a legendary king of Chios, son of Dionysus, known in myth for blinding Orion.

context_notes.text: Alexander the Great, son of Philip of Macedon, is credited with refounding Smyrna around 300 BC, in later tradition.
The Nemeses were goddesses of retribution, honoured at Smyrna in the plural, as two figures.
Rhamnus in Attica had a famous sanctuary of Nemesis.
The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
Dreams were thought to carry divine instruction, and gods often cured the sick in dreams, so Phormio's vision fits Greek religious belief.
The rule is an aetiological custom: a ritual practice explained by a founding story, here honouring the Thracian women who gave their hair.
Athene Polias means Athene as protector of the city; temples of her were common in Greek cities.
The Meles river near Smyrna was associated with Homer, whose birthplace several cities claimed.

literary_notes.text: The dream apparition of the goddesses gives divine sanction, anticipating the later oracle's approval.
"Thrice happy yea four times happy" is a rising numerical formula that intensifies the blessing in typical oracular style.
The temples are still wonderful despite the fire, a striking praise that suggests grandeur surviving ruin.
The citizen women refuse while slaves and working women give their hair, so the humbler women become the heroines of the story.
The blind man whose dream solves the problem, when the whole community failed, is rewarded with sight.
Pausanias ends the Ionian catalogue with a sweeping claim that Ionia's wonders nearly rival all of Greece.
